diagnoses.description: The skill explains graph construction and validation but does not provide an implementation-oriented workflow for parsing bracketed scene headers, speaker lines with arrow targets, numbered choices, optional bracketed choice labels, blank lines, or terminal targets. Its Edge API uses source/target while the required serialized schema uses from/to, and it does not clearly specify parse_script(text), exact node fields, deterministic IDs, reachability rules, missing-target exceptions, or dialogue.json and dialogue.dot generation.

This is central because nonzero quality flags, outliers, gaps, and strong stellar variability can conceal the transit or create false periodogram peaks. Generic sigma clipping or flattening can also remove or distort shallow, repeated transit dips.

The general workflow needs to distinguish stellar rotation or oscillation periods from the planetary orbital period and prescribe validation rather than accepting the strongest raw or residual peak. The task also requires a precise file-writing output.

TLS is the most appropriate primary detector for a shallow exoplanet transit, but it must be run on quality-filtered, activity-detrended data with uncertainty handling, suitable search bounds, and explicit checks against residual activity and aliases.

BLS is a useful independent cross-check or fallback, especially if TLS is unavailable, but it can select residual stellar variability or an alias when its period and duration grids or peak validation are underspecified.

The required TokenType, Token, BaseTokenizer, concrete tokenizer classes, UniversalTokenizer, and TokenizerBuilder make class modeling, inheritance, immutable data representation, and builder behavior central. Generic OOP guidance does not sufficiently ensure that all required Python APIs, constructors, overrides, validation rules, and helper operations such as toToken and withMetadata survive in compiling Scala 2.13.

The task explicitly requires idiomatic, maintainable Scala rather than a literal translation, while still requiring behavioral and API compatibility. The existing high-level advice lacks an integrated design for immutable tokenizer state, sealed token models, strategy/delegation, compatibility wrappers, and natural absence or error handling.

A large source-driven translation is vulnerable to compilation and semantic errors in Python annotations, defaults, conditionals, comprehensions, type checks, f-strings, exceptions, static/class methods, and None/truthiness behavior. Generic mappings do not provide enough Scala 2.13-specific guidance for the specified tokenizer API.

Tokenizer internals and especially tokenizeBatch depend on collection transformations, flattening, filtering, metadata maps, and stable ordering. Incorrect List/Seq choices, nested results, inference, or empty-input behavior can cause both compilation failures and observable mismatches with Python.

Generic Trivy guidance may not adequately specify auditing an npm package-lock.json, covering transitive dependencies, handling database or tool availability, parsing JSON findings, filtering severity, and preserving the package/version and vulnerability metadata required by the report.

The report requires a CVSS_Score for every retained vulnerability and allows NVD, GHSA, or RedHat data. Generic extraction guidance may leave source precedence, CVSS version selection, alias mapping, missing values, and reconciliation with scanner severity ambiguous, causing blank or mismatched scores.

The deliverable has a strict path, header, field mapping, severity filter, and row semantics. Generic CSV guidance may not enforce the exact column order, missing fixed-version representation, one-row-per-finding behavior, RFC-compliant escaping, or post-write validation required by the verifier.

Pause detection is the main source of false removals and boundary errors. Local one-second thresholding can mistake quiet teaching speech for silence, miss pauses when surrounding audio is also quiet, and treat a pause exactly at the duration threshold ambiguously. The detector also lacks a sufficiently explicit candidate-confirmation, boundary, and timestamp policy.

Initial-opening detection is distinct from later pause detection, but the baseline method assumes the beginning is literal silence and representative of the recording. Static or noisy title/setup footage may therefore be missed, while an initially quiet spoken introduction may be removed. The detector needs a confidence-based prefix policy rather than an unrestricted energy transition.

The processor is the decisive integration point: even correct detections can fail through overlapping cuts, invalid keep ranges, timestamp drift, A/V desynchronization, unsupported streams, or output-duration discrepancies. The workflow also needs explicit behavior for first/last cuts, no cuts, absent audio, and removal of the entire input.

The report is likely structurally evaluated as well as numerically. Detector metadata, overlapping intervals, independent duration calculations, and encoder rounding can produce extra fields, double-counted removals, or arithmetic inconsistent with the actual compressed video.
